title: Maximize Sum of Array After K Negations
description: Maximize the sum of an array after exactly k sign flips, using a sort-then-greedy-flip strategy with a final parity check.

sections.title: Maximize Sum of Array After K Negations

content.title: Maximize Sum of Array After K Negations

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, exactly k times, choose an index and replace nums[i] with -nums[i] (the same index can be chosen multiple times). Return the largest possible sum of the array after exactly k negations.

blocks.caption: Negating the most negative values first always helps; a leftover negation should hit the smallest value.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","nums[] (can contain negatives, zero), k (exact number of negations)"],["Rule","Each negation flips the sign of one element; the same element can be negated more than once"],["Output","The maximum achievable sum after exactly k negations"]]}

blocks.text: Maximizing a sum by flipping signs is a greedy problem: always flip the MOST NEGATIVE value, since turning a large negative into a large positive gains the most. Sorting the array makes finding "the most negative remaining value" trivial, since it is always the current leftmost unflipped element.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: The key subtlety once every negative becomes non-negative: any REMAINING negations must be spent somewhere, and flipping the SAME element twice cancels out (no net effect), so only the parity (odd or even) of leftover negations matters, and an odd leftover should target the SMALLEST value to minimize the loss.

Picture a ledger of debts (negative values) and credits (positive values). Flipping a debt into a credit is always beneficial, and the bigger the debt, the more is gained by flipping it. Once every debt has been flipped, if any flips remain, they must be spent somewhere; flipping the SAME value back and forth wastes flips with no net change, so any single leftover flip should target the SMALLEST remaining value, since that loses the least.

blocks.caption: Flip the biggest debts first; a leftover single flip should hit the smallest remaining value.

items: Sort the array ascending, so the most negative values come first.
Flip values from the front while they are still negative and k allows, always the greedy-optimal choice.
If k negations remain (some possibly "wasted" flipping the same value back and forth), only the PARITY matters: an even leftover changes nothing, an odd leftover flips the smallest value once.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Array","k remaining","Action"],"rows":[["Start","[-1,0,2,3]","3","-"],["Flip -1","[1,0,2,3]","2","the only negative value, flipped"],["No more negatives","[1,0,2,3]","2","stop the negation phase"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: With 2 negations remaining (even), they cancel out with no net effect (flip the same value twice). Sum = 1+0+2+3 = 6, matching the expected output.

A direct simulation repeatedly finds the current minimum value and flips it, one negation at a time, k times total. This directly implements the greedy rule but re-scans the whole array on every single step.

Sorting once up front lets the negation phase proceed left to right in a single pass (each element is only ever the "current minimum" once it is reached in sorted order), and the leftover-negations phase reduces to a simple parity check plus one final adjustment, avoiding repeated re-scanning.
Repeatedly scan for the current minimum value and flip its sign, k times total.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(k * n)","Each of the k negations rescans the array to find the current minimum"],["Space","O(n)","The working copy of the array"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: When k is large, repeatedly rescanning the whole array for the minimum is unnecessary once sorting establishes a fixed processing order.

Sort the array. Walk left to right, flipping negative values while k allows. Once the negatives are exhausted (or k runs out), sum the array; if k negations remain, subtract twice the array's minimum value if k is odd (an even leftover has no net effect).

items: Sort the array, O(n log n).
Flip negative values from the front while k allows, O(n).
Sum the array; if leftover k is odd, subtract 2 times the minimum value (undoing one flip on it).

codes.python:
def largest_sum_after_k_negations(nums, k):
    arr = sorted(nums)
    i = 0

    while i < len(arr) and k > 0 and arr[i] < 0:
        arr[i] = -arr[i]
        i += 1
        k -= 1

    total = sum(arr)
    if k % 2 == 1:
        total -= 2 * min(arr)

    return total


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(largest_sum_after_k_negations([4, 2, 3], 1))
    print(largest_sum_after_k_negations([3, -1, 0, 2], 3))

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, repeated min-scan","O(k * n)","O(n)"],["Optimized, sort + single pass","O(n log n)","O(n)"]]}

items: Sorting turns "always flip the current minimum" into a simple single left-to-right pass, since the minimum is always the next unprocessed element.
Flipping the same value an even number of times has no net effect, so only the PARITY of leftover operations matters once no more beneficial flips remain.
When forced to "waste" a leftover odd operation, targeting the value that loses the LEAST (the current minimum) is the correct greedy choice.

blocks.text: Maximize Sum of Array After K Negations is solved by sorting the array and greedily flipping negative values from the front while negations remain. Once no negatives remain, only the parity of leftover negations matters: an odd leftover subtracts twice the array's current minimum from the sum, giving an O(n log n) solution.
